programmeLevelAssessment: The strongest proposed UCR programme is coherent and feasible, with 12 biomedical courses (90 EC), 10 mathematics/computing courses (75 EC), introductory research methods (7.5 EC) and mandatory PPD (7.5 EC). Its substantial physiology, biochemical/molecular disease study, molecular laboratory work and quantitative/image-analysis contributions are preserved. They do not implement the defining integration of experimental medical physics, physical chemistry and physiological measurement in this degree. VU physics practicals combine experiments, error analysis and Python/MATLAB; later work includes ultrasound/interferometry and physical measurement models. Optics treats wave propagation, interference, diffraction and lasers; radiation/audiology uses physical models; quantum-to-molecule study links microscopic theory and spectroscopy to medical applications. Clinical analytical chemistry teaches extraction, chromatography, spectroscopy and mass spectrometry. UCR image processing explicitly includes medical applications, but processing an image is not the physics of acquiring it. Its machine learning, database and neural-network courses do not supply molecular-network dynamics, sequence/transcriptomics analysis or measured physiological signal modelling. Life Science Laboratory has genuine PCR, ELISA, protein and introductory bioinformatics work, not a substitute for the physical measurement/analytical-chemistry sequence. A reconstruction from actual sustainability content was tested: Sustainability Essentials introduces physics/chemistry in planetary-boundary problems and R3 includes inorganic chemistry and resource-recovery laboratory skills. Those are real contributions, so the prior statement that UCR has no physics or chemistry at all is false; their purpose and progression do not remedy the missing medical-physical/analytical sequence. Reweighting the same biomedical and data courses would change the organising inquiry to biomedical or health-data science. No complete substantive UCR response to this integrated target is established; this is not based merely on a degree title, professional licence, an absent individual course, or a matching quota.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Personal & Professional Development
preservedCourseContributions.content: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives

preservedCourseContributions.name: Research Methods & Statistics
preservedCourseContributions.content: Research Methods & Statistics is a general introduction in research methodology and statistics. The introduction to methodology includes the logics and design of research (e.g., operationalization, experimental design, sampling), and some specific techniques (e.g., laboratory research, surveys). The introduction to statistics includes descriptive and inferential statistics, covering measures of central tendency, spread, association, univariate and bivariate inferential statistics, and analysis of variance. This course includes an introduction to simple applications of multivariate statistics but most coverage of multivariate statistics and statistical modelling will be covered in the course HCBPSYC211 Statistics & Experimental Methods in Health & Behavioral Sciences. The first 9 course weeks (not including the semester break) of the course provide the theoretical background. This includes not only instruction and practice in basic research methodology and statistics, but also the planning stages of the group research projects that will dominate the latter portion of the semester. In this portion of the semester, students of each section attend two classes each week with their instructor. Project groups are formed, and these groups work together in applying newly learned concepts to their own research problem thru individually completed homework exercises, and through sharing and discussing their progress with the rest of the class. The final 6 course weeks are dedicated exclusively to group project work. This research project can fall within any academic discipline.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Introduction to Data Science
preservedCourseContributions.content: Data science provides tools for extracting meaningful information from data. In this course, you develop foundational abilities in data visualization as well as data cleaning and manipulation. Next to traditional data coming in the form of tables, we explore non-traditional data types such as spatial data and text data. The course includes much hands -on work with example data sets coming from sciences, social sciences, and arts and humanities. At the end of the course, you carry out your own research project in which you apply your data analysis and visualization skills to answer a research question.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Machine Learning
preservedCourseContributions.content: Machine learning concerns an ever -expanding set of tools for understanding data and making predictions. This course introduces the fundamentals of machine learning. It presents several of the most important modelling and prediction techniques, along with several relevant applications. Topics include linear regression, classification, resampling methods, shrinkage approaches, tree - based methods, support vector machines, clustering, and more. Real-world examples are used to illustrate the methods, their strengths, and their limitations.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Image Processing & Computer Vision
preservedCourseContributions.content: Image Processing and Computer Vision deals with extracting high-level structural understanding from digital image and video data. As such, it aims to automate the task of the human visual system. In the broadest sense, Image Processing and Computer Vision studies methods for acquiring, processing, analysis, and understanding of image data. The course starts with a concise introduction into cameras, color models, and various image models and representations, but focuses on the processing, analysis, and understanding of image data. Image processing and analysis have many applications, inside as well as outside of robotics. An important application domain is medical imaging, where the goal is to reveal internal structures to diagnose and treat disease. Another application is remote sensing which aims to detect objects on earth. Image processing and analysis study methods that turn images into better images and aim to identify simple features in images. The course considers histograms, point operators, and local, edge, and morphological filters. It covers the Hough transform for detection of lines and curves, detection of corners, shapes and regions, and segmentation. Image understanding concerns the recognition of objects in images. The course introduces feature detection and tracking and object localization, classification, and evaluation. The Image Processing and Computer Vision course offers ample time to practice with the image processing, image analysis, and image understanding methods that are presented.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
preservedCourseContributions.content: Neural networks have enabled major advances in areas such as computer vision, large language models, and generative AI. This course focuses on the underlying theory as well as practical implementations in the Python programming language using packages such as TensorFlow . No familiarity with Python is assumed, but a willingness to learn and write code in Python is essential. In the first part of the course, w e start by building and training our own basic neural networks from scratch. We also use TensorFlow to create bigger networks and apply them to tabular data. In the second part of the course, we move on to more complex neural networks for applications such as computer vision and text classification . We also discuss recent developments in large language models (such as ChatGPT) . Finally, if time per mits, we have a brief look at image generation models (such as DALL-E).

preservedCourseContributions.name: Introduction to Programming
preservedCourseContributions.content: This is the gateway course of Computer Science and AI studies; an introductory course in problem solving and computer programming in Python. The course begins by introducing traditional structured programming and data constructs (i.e. branching, loops, functions; tuples and lists). Then consideration is given to testing and debugging and finally the object- oriented programming constructs. During the entire semester, elements of discrete mathematics (e.g., logic, sets, enumeration) as well as certain computational problem solving techniques are also incorporated into the course material. There are classes twice a week. The first half of each class is a lecture where we learn new material, while the second half is devoted to laboratory work where students tackle programming exercises and demonstrate their work. Homework comprises weekly programming exercises and online quizzes. Two larger programming projects are undertaken. There is a written Midterm exam and a written Final exam. By the end of the course a student will have obtained a reasonable familiarity with the Python programming language as well as important concepts of discrete mathematics and computational problem solving techniques.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Mathematical Methods
preservedCourseContributions.content: Mathematics is the language used to grasp understanding of, to explore, and to gain insight in any of the sciences: physics, chemistry, biology, as well as engineering. None of these can be well understood or appreciated without sufficient skills in mathematics. The aim of this introductory course in the mathematics track is to learn basic widely-used mathematical techniques, such as differentiation, various techniques for integration, complex numbers and differential equations. These techniques are put into context in projects related to real situations in the fields of physics, chemistry, biology, economics, sociology, etc. In this course students will continue to construct knowledge on their mathematical bases already founded. Students will solve many problems as homework assignments. Furthermore, two exams will assess the students for their level of understanding and their ability to solve relevant mathematical problems. A lot of class time will be used to solve and discuss textbook problems. 3

preservedCourseContributions.name: Linear Algebra
preservedCourseContributions.content: Linear algebra is the study of systems of linear equations and linear functions. Systematic methods exist to solve such systems of linear equations. Matrices and vectors are introduced as the equivalent of a system of linear equations. This equivalence allows for reducing problems involving linear combinations of vectors to questions about systems of linear equations. The spanning of a (sub)space, linear independence and linear transformations are fundamental concepts in linear algebra. Matrix operations and theorems involving matrices will provide the basic tools for handling many applications of linear algebra. The invertible matrix theorem is a theorem of particular importance. The determinant of a matrix is an important scalar quantity related to the invertibility criterion for square matrices. Furthermore, the determinant is a measure for the amount by which a linear transformation changes the area of a ﬁgure. In multi-variable calculus, this measure is deﬁned as the Jacobian of a transformation. Introducing the more abstract concept of vector spaces allows for further generalization of these ideas. Many vector spaces resemble the well-known vector space Rn. In this course, the theory of vector spaces will be applied to the processing of discrete signals (Fourier Series), diﬀerence equations and Markov chains. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors are used to understand the action of a linear transformation. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors arise naturally in diﬀerent areas of physics and mathematics.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Computational & Numerical Methods
preservedCourseContributions.content: Many problems in science and engineering presented in a mathematical format do not have exact analyt- ical solutions; these problems can only be solved numerically. The nature of the mathematical problem dictates the type of numerical algorithm to use; solving an optimization problem requires a different al- gorithm than solving a differential equation. The prerequisite gateway courseMathematical Methods introduces techniques and methods for solving equations in one variable, for finding derivatives of func- tions, or for solving integrals,etc., analytically. This course focuses on the same mathematical concepts but from a numerical and computational perspective. Numerical solutions obtained through some al- gorithm pose the following challenge: what does the output mean? How sensitive is the algorithm to a wrong input? There are examples showing that numerical algorithms can produce completely wrong and unexpected outputs resulting in a disaster. Numerical and computational mathematics is a broad topic; numerous algorithms exist for numerically solving the same mathematical problem. This courses focuses on algorithms for solving equations in one variable. Several algorithms exist for interpolating or extrapolating functions on the basis of a set of sample points of that function. Numerical methods for differentiation, but especially integration form a set of very important numerical algorithms. The course discusses numerous algorithms for solving ordinary differential equations.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Probability & Statistics
preservedCourseContributions.content: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Epidemiology & Public Health
preservedCourseContributions.content: Public health is about changing the world. From pandemics to lifestyle-related diseases, from screening for disease to improving water and air quality, it asks: how can we improve to keep the population healthy?_x000D_ But how do we know what actually works? In this course you will dive into epidemiology: the science behind public health. You will learn how to study disease, risks, and changes over time, and how to critically evaluate evidence. Because behind every public health decision lies a question of evidence, and by the end of this course, you will be equipped to engage with it. This course invites you to look beyond the lab, the hospital, and the library, into the wider world where health is shaped. What matters most if we truly care about health, and how can we influence that?

preservedCourseContributions.name: Functional Anatomy
preservedCourseContributions.content: Functional Anatomy examines the structure of the human body in direct relation to function. In this course, anatomical structures and their functions are systematically studied together, at the level of body systems as well as individual anatomical components. The course is organised in thematic blocks, each addressing a specific anatomical region or system (the Skeletal System & Vertebral Column; Bony Thorax & Pelvis; Respiratory & Cardiovascular Systems; Abdomen; Reproductive & Lower Urinary Systems) and each emphasising specific anatomical and functional reasoning (rather than exhaustive memorisation). Within these blocks, learning activities are purposefully selected to support the intended learning outcomes, combining visual, spatial and experiential approaches. Anatomical understanding is developed through surface anatomy, medical imaging, scientific anatomical drawing and video-based human remain based material, complemented by carefully framed encounters with human skeletal remains, a dissection facility and in class clinical demonstrations. Together, these activities foster three-dimensional anatomical insight, spatial reasoning and awareness of anatomical variation. Please note that these are explicitly framed as academic learning experiences rather than clinical skills training. Studying human anatomy inevitably confronts students with an ethical paradox: respect for the human body is taught through its objectification for scientific study.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Pharmacology
preservedCourseContributions.content: Pharmacology is the science of drugs including their origin, composition, pharmacokinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity (Merriam-Webster Learner’s Dictionary). The functioning of the (diseased) human body can be affected by (medicinal) drugs, which act through a variety of molecular mechanisms. In this course, the basic principles of pharmacology will be discussed, followed by studies of different aspects of drugs and the human body to illustrate the se pharmacological principles which are used for rational drug develo pment and physiological use. The importance of neuronal, hormonal, immunological (whole body) and biochemical (whole cell) regulation for proper physiological and cellular function, and dysregulation during pathological processes are emphasized. Identification of potential drug t argets and the interaction of drugs with macromolecules (enzymes, cell surface receptors, and signaling molecules) as the main pharmacological principles are central in this course. Quantitative pharmacological, pharmacokinetic and statistical methods are used. At the end of the course you will be able to explain effectiv ely existing drug therapies in a rational way in terms of molecular targets, cellular actions and physiological consequences of pharmacological treatment. They will be able to suggest targets for drug development on the basis of pathophysiological insights a nd to apply pharmacological models when describing concentration-response, time-concentration, and time-response relationships of drugs.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Infection & Immunity
preservedCourseContributions.content: Infectious diseases and disorders of the immune system are a continuous threat to the life and well-being of humans, animals and plants. Studying the fundamental processes in immunology, such as the recognition of self and non-self (e.g. microbes), development of mature lymphocyte receptor repertoires, and the innate and adaptive immune response is crucial for the understanding how the immune system deals with the daily threat of microorganisms. On the other hand, general knowledge of the highly diverse mic robial world is needed. From this knowledge, detailed specific understanding of microbial strategies to circumvent host resistance can be acquired. As a principle, the course will focus on interactions between host and infectious agents. Basic principles a s microbial virulence, inflammatory responses, tissue damage and apoptosis are discussed. In addition to normal immune responses to infectious agents, the course will also deal with immunopathological processes and diseases.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Mechanisms of Disease
preservedCourseContributions.content: In this course the relation between the normal function (physiology) and disease (pathophysiology) is illustrated for six basal organ systems: 1. cardiovascular, 2. lung (pulmonology), 3. kidney (nephrology), 4. digestive tract, 5. endocrine glands (endocrinology) and 6. central nervous system. The aim of this course is to provide insight in the principles of the mechanisms of diseases. For the organ systems mentioned the student first has to study the embryology and anatomy, Using this information as starting point, the basic physiology is studied and using the combined knowledge the student must be able to derive the symptoms and failures in the system or the pathophysiology.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Neurobiology
preservedCourseContributions.content: Cognitive neuroscience uses inputs and perspectives from many disciplines, such as psychology, biology, medicine, computer science, and philosophy. In this course, the focus will be on the biology side of neuroscience. As a result, we will focus on evoluti onary pressures on animals in general, resulting in specific behaviors and physiological processes in these animals and ourselves. In this light, you will gain a greater understanding of biorhythms and natural behaviors, and eventually of specific disorders and diseases. Additionally, we will take a look at the use of animals in neuroscientific research, such as rodents, and discuss ethical and welfare implications. We will also familiarize you with experimental techniques in the laboratory, such as cell st aining and using a microscope, and compare the (brain) anatomy of different animal species. This course will familiarize you with concepts and skills required within the discipline of Neurobiology. A selected number of key topics within the field will be discussed, including comparative anatomy, biorhythms, animal models and ethics, and disorders . The course also includes guest lectures and practical work such as labwork, group assignments and student presentations.
preservedCourseContributions.assessment: Specific contribution preserved; no unqualified replacement of defining medical physics/chemistry.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
preservedCourseContributions.content: Have you ever wondered what makes life on earth possible? The foundation of life, health & biomedical science course takes you on a journey into the building blocks of life, exploring how cells, molecules, and systems interact to create and sustain living organisms. Cells are at the heart of this story: they are the basic units of life, taking in energy and nutrients from their environment and converting them into biologically useful forms. Inside every cell lies genetic information, dna, that not only directs all cellular activities but also passes traits from one generation to the next. Mutations, recombination and epigenetics create variation, and this diversity fuels the evolutionary process through natural selection. The course is structured in four interconnected units: The cell as a unit of life Basic molecular biology Cellular physiology and communication Capita selecta (a series of explorations that give you a first taste of the diverse academic pathways in biomedical sciences, life sciences, medicine, and public health.) You will also work on a special research presentation assignment, which allows you to engage with scientific literature, reflect on how we know what we know, and experience how new knowledge can be generated. But this course is more than just an introduction. As a gateway course, foundation of life, health & biomedical science opens the door to exciting academic pathways in biomedical sciences, life sciences, medicine, and public health.
preservedCourseContributions.assessment: Specific contribution preserved; no unqualified replacement of defining medical physics/chemistry.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Molecular Cell Biology
preservedCourseContributions.content: New discoveries and advancements in scientific research are proposed every day, all around us. It can be overwhelming to keep up. This course provides the foundation for students to understand a vast array of practical applications in a multitude of life science topics (e.g. industry, medicine, agriculture, ecology, etc.). Students w ill take a closer look at the cellular biology of mostly eukaryotes, but also prokaryotes, gaining a comprehensive understanding of cell structure and physio logy. Concepts from the LIFE101 course, Introduction to Life Sciences, will be revisited and students will dive deeper into the details of life processes to understand the underlying molecular mechanisms. Students will also learn to examine current research topics and methods used to study the invisible world of molecular biology. Students will be encouraged to question the reproducibility of results and to propose how modernization of existing methods (and/or theoretical) technologies would improve the limitations of research and the validity of results. The course consists of five themes: 1 – The fundamental units of life: Cellular components, chemistry and energetics 2 – Genomes: DNA to Proteins, replication, repair and regulation of gene expression 3 – Cellular dynamics: Membrane trafficking, transport and signaling pathways 4 – Cell fate: Cell division, tissues, stem cells and cancer 5 – Drug Mechanisms (Paper and Poster Project)
preservedCourseContributions.assessment: Specific contribution preserved; no unqualified replacement of defining medical physics/chemistry.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Human Physiology
preservedCourseContributions.content: Physiology is the study of the normal functioning of a living organism and its component parts, including all its chemical and physical processes. In this course, the focus is on the function of the adult human body and of different organ systems. Knowledge of the subject is essential for students with a medical interest and recommended for every student interested in the function (s) of the (own) human body. The course includes fundamental concepts of molecules, cellular and systems physiology to understand how the human body functions and maintains a steady state. Although some medical examples are used to illustrate general physiological principles, this is not a course in medical physiology. Still, the core of physiological knowledge you will learn by ta king Human Physiology will help you better understand human health and disease. The course will be divided in 4 units: (1) Basic cell processes , (2) Homeostasis and control, (3) Integration of function , and (4) Metabolism, growth, and aging . In addition there will be one individual assignment. Contents of the 4 course units are structure-function relationships (organelles, cells, tissues, organs), energy handling, homeostasis and control systems, signaling and communication, study of individual organ systems (cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine, muscles, nervous, digestive, reproduction), and integration of functions.
preservedCourseContributions.assessment: Specific contribution preserved; no unqualified replacement of defining medical physics/chemistry.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Biochemistry
preservedCourseContributions.content: Living organisms evolved from the prebiotic world through chemical reactions. Laws governing those early reactions are the same t oday. C hemistry is the underlying science behind biology. Biochemistry, the chemistry of life, deals with the reactions that produce the molecules of life: proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids that enable the self -assembly and reproduction of simple and complex organisms. Although organisms vary en ormously in complexity and biological properties, all domains of life use similar biomolecules for encoding and transmitting information, intra - and intercellular signaling, formation of membranes, building and degrading macromolecules, energy metabolism, and many more features. Errors in the production, proper localization or degradation of these molecules can often lead to disease. Biochemical knowledge is not only essential for understanding and treating these diseases, but also necessary for advancing many applications in biotechnology.
preservedCourseContributions.assessment: Specific contribution preserved; no unqualified replacement of defining medical physics/chemistry.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Life Science Laboratory
preservedCourseContributions.content: This course is designed for a broad group of UCR students interested in life sciences. This course provides an introduction to the biochemical and molecular laboratory work performed in most labs today, and hence is a highly recommended course for all life science and medical track students. The students will be introduced to the following themes: • Blood • Bacteria, handling hygiene and genetically modified organisms (GMOs) • Protein production, isolation and analysis • DNA isolation and analysis (digestion, PCR and gel electrophoresis) • Bioinformatics These themes are characteristic or representative of basic biological and clinical research. Additional clinical diagnostic themes are added whenever there is an opportunity. The concepts, principles and techniques used in this course regarding blood and blood proteins include a basic blood cell analysis (hemogram), protein electrophoresis, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and a patient case. Course outline HCBLIFE214; Life Science Laboratory Page 2 of 8 With respect to bacteria, students will first learn the skills for properly handling pure cultures. A series of tests will also be carried out to check hygiene and sterilization procedures, bacterial species determination and the effect of antibiotics on bacterial growth. It also includes genetic modification of bacteria using safe microbiological techniques. After students have become acquainted with the safe handling of bacteria, they will generate a genetically modified organism (GMO).

preservedCourseContributions.name: Molecular Pathology & Genetics
preservedCourseContributions.content: This course covers a vast number of topics from general and molecular pathology and genetics of humans. The pathology portion includes the bases of pathology which is cell injury and cell death. The pathology also covers how acute and chronic inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration and fibrosis, and neoplasia contribute to pathologies. The course then shifts to understanding the molecular genetics underlying disease. The significance of chromosome structure and organization of genes will be covered along with gene mutations (and their inheritance) through several examples of genetic diseases. The course also focuses on the status of genetic testing and genetic treatments. Ethical and legal considerations for now and in the future will also be examined.

preservedCourseContributions.content: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.

preservedCourseContributions.name: Sustainability Essentials I
preservedCourseContributions.content: ENSGATE101 - Sustainability Essentials serves as the Gateway course to all 200 level courses in the Environment and Sustainability Cluster. For that purpose we will discuss the tools and knowledge you need to follow and enjoy all 200 level course in the cluster. We will use the model of planetary boundaries to discuss the concepts of sustainability with an anthropogenic focus. The planetary boundaries concept was presented in 2009 and provides a novel synthesis of the most pertinent global environmental challenges by analysing the risk of crossing critical thresholds in the behaviour of the Earth system’s processes. These boundaries act as a framework to define a "safe operating space for humanity," highlighting the limits within which human development can occur without causing catastrophic harm to the planet. 3
